{{DISPLAYTITLE:Metaprogramming in Lean}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Tactics}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

A '''metaprogram''' is a Lean program whose data is Lean itself: syntax, terms, goals,
Lean's environment (its table of definitions and theorems). Tactics, elaborators and
custom commands are metaprograms. Lean 4 is written largely in Lean, and the data
structures and functions its own elaborator and tactics use are available to any Lean source
file that imports the library <code>Lean</code>.<ref name="cade">Leonardo de Moura and Sebastian Ullrich, "The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language (System Description)", in ''Automated Deduction: CADE 28'', Lecture Notes in Computer Science 12699, Springer, 2021, pp. 625–635. doi:[https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37 10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37]; author's copy [https://lean-lang.org/papers/lean4.pdf lean-lang.org/papers/lean4.pdf].</ref>
This page shows the representation of terms, the monads metaprograms run in, and three small
metaprograms compiled by Lean 4.34.1: a term elaborator, a command and a tactic. It ends with
the point on which the whole arrangement rests. A metaprogram is not trusted. What it
produces is checked by the Lean kernel, and a wrong result is rejected, unless that check has
been switched off.

== Terms as data ==

Every term that reaches the Lean kernel is a value of the inductive type
<code>Lean.Expr</code>. Lean prints its definition on request.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
import Lean
open Lean Meta Elab Term Command Tactic

#print Lean.Expr
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">inductive Lean.Expr : Type
number of parameters: 0
constructors:
Lean.Expr.bvar : Nat → Expr
Lean.Expr.fvar : FVarId → Expr
Lean.Expr.mvar : MVarId → Expr
Lean.Expr.sort : Level → Expr
Lean.Expr.const : Name → List Level → Expr
Lean.Expr.app : Expr → Expr → Expr
Lean.Expr.lam : Name → Expr → Expr → BinderInfo → Expr
Lean.Expr.forallE : Name → Expr → Expr → BinderInfo → Expr
Lean.Expr.letE : Name → Expr → Expr → Expr → Bool → Expr
Lean.Expr.lit : Literal → Expr
Lean.Expr.mdata : MData → Expr → Expr
Lean.Expr.proj : Name → Nat → Expr → Expr</pre>

The twelve constructors are the type theory's term formers with some additions for
practical use. <code>sort</code> is a universe, <code>const</code> a reference to a named
definition or theorem at given universe levels, <code>app</code> an application,
<code>lam</code> a function, <code>forallE</code> a dependent function type and
<code>letE</code> a local definition. <code>lit</code> holds a natural-number or string
literal, <code>proj</code> a projection from a structure, and <code>mdata</code> attaches
metadata that does not change meaning. Three constructors are variables of different
kinds. <code>bvar</code> is a variable bound inside the term, named by a number, the
'''de Bruijn index''', which counts binders outward; <code>fvar</code> is a free variable
of the current local context, such as a hypothesis in a goal; <code>mvar</code> is a
'''metavariable''', a hole still to be filled (see
[[Lean theorem prover/System/Metavariables and unification|metavariables and unification]]).

A small definition shows the encoding.

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def k : Nat → Nat → Nat := fun a _b => a

#eval show MetaM Unit from do
  let info ← getConstInfo ``k
  IO.println (repr info.value!)
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">Lean.Expr.lam
  `a
  (Lean.Expr.const `Nat [])
  (Lean.Expr.lam `_b (Lean.Expr.const `Nat []) (Lean.Expr.bvar 1) (Lean.BinderInfo.default))
  (Lean.BinderInfo.default)</pre>

The body of the inner function is <code>bvar 1</code>: the variable bound one binder further
out than the nearest, which is <code>a</code>. Binder names are kept only for display: two
terms that differ only in the names of bound variables are treated as the same term.

== The monads ==

A metaprogram runs in a monad that gives it access to the state of Lean (see
[[Lean theorem prover/System/Monads and do-notation|monads and do-notation]] for monads in
general). There is a stack of four, each extending the one below it. Lean prints their
definitions.

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#print CoreM
#print MetaM
#print TermElabM
#print TacticM
#print CommandElabM
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">@[reducible] def Lean.Core.CoreM : Type → Type :=
ReaderT Core.Context (StateRefT' IO.RealWorld Core.State (EIO Exception))
@[reducible] def Lean.Meta.MetaM : Type → Type :=
ReaderT Meta.Context (StateRefT' IO.RealWorld Meta.State CoreM)
@[reducible] def Lean.Elab.Term.TermElabM : Type → Type :=
ReaderT Term.Context (StateRefT' IO.RealWorld Term.State MetaM)
@[reducible] def Lean.Elab.Tactic.TacticM : Type → Type :=
ReaderT Tactic.Context (StateRefT' IO.RealWorld Tactic.State TermElabM)
@[reducible] def Lean.Elab.Command.CommandElabM : Type → Type :=
ReaderT Command.Context (StateRefT' IO.RealWorld Command.State (EIO Exception))</pre>

Each layer adds a read-only context (<code>ReaderT</code>) and a mutable state
(<code>StateRefT'</code>) on top of the layer below. At the bottom, <code>EIO
Exception</code> is input and output that can fail with an exception, so every metaprogram
can do input and output.

* '''<code>CoreM</code>''' gives access to Lean's environment: what has been defined or imported at the current point.
* '''<code>MetaM</code>''' adds the metavariable context, the metavariables in existence and their assignments, and with it the operations of type inference (<code>inferType</code>), reduction (<code>whnf</code>) and definitional-equality checking (<code>isDefEq</code>).
* '''<code>TermElabM</code>''' adds the information the elaborator uses while turning syntax into terms.
* '''<code>TacticM</code>''' adds the list of current goals.<ref name="mpb">Arthur Paulino, Damiano Testa, Edward Ayers, Evgenia Karunus, Henrik Böving, Jannis Limperg, Siddhartha Gadgil and Siddharth Bhat, ''Metaprogramming in Lean 4'', online book, chapter "MetaM". [https://leanprover-community.github.io/lean4-metaprogramming-book/main/04_metam.html leanprover-community.github.io/lean4-metaprogramming-book/main/04_metam.html]</ref>

<code>CommandElabM</code>, the monad of commands, stands beside the stack and not on top of
it; a command that needs to elaborate a term enters <code>TermElabM</code> with
<code>liftTermElabM</code>, as in the second example below.

== Elaborators ==

An '''elaborator''' gives meaning to a piece of syntax by running Lean code. A term
elaborator has type <code>Syntax → Option Expr → TermElabM Expr</code>: it receives the
syntax and the expected type if one is known, and must return a <code>Lean.Expr</code>. A
command elaborator has type <code>Syntax → CommandElabM Unit</code> and acts by side
effects, such as adding constants or reporting messages.<ref name="rm-elab">"Elaborators", section 23.6 of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0). [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Notations-and-Macros/Elaborators/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Notations-and-Macros/Elaborators/]</ref>
The <code>elab</code> command declares the syntax and its elaborator together.

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
elab "double! " t:term : term => do
  let stx ← `(2 * $t)
  elabTerm stx (some (mkConst ``Nat))

#eval double! 21
</pre>

This prints <code>42</code>. The elaborator constructs syntax with a quotation,
<code>`(2 * $t)</code>, and hands it to <code>elabTerm</code> with the expected type
<code>Nat</code>. Quotations are available in every one of these monads; a quotation of a
category other than terms names it, as in <code>`(tactic| intro h)</code>. Their hygiene is
the hygiene of [[Lean theorem prover/System/Syntax extension and hygienic macros|macros]].
Unlike a macro, which can do no more with Lean's environment than check whether a name exists
and resolve names, an elaborator can consult types, the local context and the whole of Lean's
environment.<ref name="rm-macros">"Macros", section 23.5 of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0), subsection 23.5.2 "The Macro Monad". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/]</ref>

A command that elaborates a term, puts it in weak head normal form and reports the result:

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
elab "#whnf " t:term : command => do
  liftTermElabM do
    let e ← elabTerm t none
    let r ← whnf e
    logInfo m!"{e} reduces to {r} : {← inferType e}"

#whnf (fun (x : Nat) => x + 1) 41
#whnf (fun (x : Nat) => [x, x]) 7
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">(fun x => x + 1) 41 reduces to 42 : Nat
(fun x => [x, x]) 7 reduces to [7, 7] : List Nat</pre>

== A tactic ==

A tactic is an elaborator in <code>TacticM</code> (the
[[Lean theorem prover/System/The tactic framework|tactic framework]] describes how they are
run). This one closes the main goal with any hypothesis whose type is definitionally equal
to it, a simple form of Lean's <code>assumption</code>.

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
elab "my_assumption" : tactic => do
  let goal ← getMainGoal
  let target ← goal.getType
  for h in ← getLCtx do
    if !h.isImplementationDetail &amp;&amp; (← isDefEq h.type target) then
      goal.assign h.toExpr
      replaceMainGoal []
      return
  throwError "my_assumption: no hypothesis has type {target}"

example (p q : Prop) (hp : p) (hq : q) : p ∧ q :=
  ⟨by my_assumption, by my_assumption⟩
</pre>

Each goal is a metavariable, and closing it means assigning it a term: here the free
variable <code>hp</code> for the first goal and <code>hq</code> for the second. When no
hypothesis fits, the tactic fails with its own message:

<pre class="lean lean-cont lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example (p q : Prop) (hp : p) : q := by my_assumption
</pre>

Lean reports <code>my_assumption: no hypothesis has type q</code>.

== Metaprograms are not trusted ==

Nothing stops a tactic from assigning a goal a term of the wrong type. The assignment
operation does not check. This tactic claims to prove anything with <code>True.intro</code>,
the proof of <code>True</code>.

<pre class="lean lean-cont lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
elab "cheat" : tactic => do
  let goal ← getMainGoal
  goal.assign (mkConst ``True.intro)
  replaceMainGoal []

theorem bad : False := by cheat
</pre>

The tactic runs and reports no failure, but the theorem is refused:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">(kernel) declaration type mismatch, 'bad' has type
  True
but it is expected to have type
  False</pre>

The message is the Lean kernel's. When a definition or theorem is complete, the elaborator
passes it to the Lean kernel, which checks it against the rules of the type theory before it
enters Lean's environment. The reference manual states the purpose plainly: the elaborator's
output must be checked by the Lean kernel "to guard against potential bugs in
elaboration".<ref name="rm-ec">"Elaboration and Compilation", a chapter of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0), section "The Kernel". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation/]</ref>
The elaborator, the tactic framework, the simplifier and every user's tactic are outside the
trusted part of the system. They may be wrong, and, as long as the Lean kernel's check is not
switched off, a wrong result costs a failed check, not a false theorem.

This is why metaprogramming can be open to every user. A proof assistant whose automation
had to be trusted would have to restrict who may write automation, or audit it. Lean instead
lets any file define tactics and elaborators with the same access its own have, because the
check at the end does not depend on how the term was found.

The guarantee has limits, and they are worth stating. The check covers only what reaches
the Lean kernel. The option <code>debug.skipKernelTC</code> switches it off, and code run during
elaboration can add a constant to Lean's environment without passing it to the Lean kernel;
the reference manual names both as ways of bypassing the check.<ref name="rm-validating" /> With
that option set, the <code>cheat</code> tactic above yields an accepted theorem
<code>bad : False</code>. A metaprogram runs with the full rights of input and output, and the
reference manual's guidance on validating a proof warns that tactics and other code run at
elaboration "can perform arbitrary actions when run", including, in the hostile case,
interfering with the system before any check takes place.<ref name="rm-validating">"Validating a Lean Proof", a chapter of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0). [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs/]</ref>
Honest mistakes are caught by the check above. Deliberate tampering is the subject of
[[Lean theorem prover/System/Proof export and independent checkers|proof export and independent checkers]].
